title: 3D-MoE: Complementarity-Guided Hardware-Software Co-Design for MoE Decode on 3D-Stacked NMP
summary:
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) have become a mainstream way to scale Large Language Models (LLMs), because each token activates only a small subset of experts, reducing inference cost. However, MoE decode remains highly memory-bound and exhibits strongly skewed, time-varying expert loads. 3D-stacked DRAM near-memory processing (NMP) provides the bandwidth that decode demands, yet its tiled organization makes load balancing expensive: expert parallelism (EP) preserves locality but suffers from hotspot-induced imbalance, while more distributed strategies weaken locality and increase NoC traffic.
  To address this locality-balance conflict, we observe that domain-specialized token routing creates offsetting expert-load fluctuations across decode steps, a property we call expert complementarity. Using this insight, we propose 3D-MoE, a hardware--software co-designed system for MoE decode on 3D-stacked NMP. 3D-MoE uses offline, one-time complementarity-guided grouping and locality-aware mapping to establish coarse-grained inter-group balance, handles residual intra-group hotspots through a lightweight Collaborative Memory-Network (CMN) that streams each hot expert's weight tiles once from its host DRAM channel to helper cores over a reconfigured local broadcast path, and uses cost-aware online remapping to remain robust to workload drift. Across MoE models, 3D-MoE achieves an average 4.63$\times$ MoE-layer speedup over EP and improves end-to-end throughput by 1.58$\times$--1.86$\times$ over the strongest NMP baselines, with 2.11\% additional logic-die area.

title: Sustainable Processing-in-DRAM Integration and Replacement for Transformer Inference Servers
summary: Processing-in-DRAM (PID) accelerators are emerging as a sustainable alternative to GPUs for transformer model inference. They bring compute to data, mitigate the memory bandwidth limitation, and reduce the overall energy footprint. Yet, carbon analysis of PID accelerators is covered for only a limited set of hardware and workloads. In this work, we present a carbon modeling framework for PID-enabled inference servers that captures embodied carbon along with idle and active operational carbon. Our evaluation spans three GPU baselines, six PID architectures, and eight transformer workloads. Additionally, we propose an aging-aware model that finds the carbon-optimal replacement period for PID accelerators over a 10-year horizon. Across evaluated configurations, our analysis shows that including PIDs in AI inference servers increases the total embodied carbon by at most 2.5\%, while the total carbon is reduced by up to 1.14$\times$ for encoder and 1.04$\times$ for decoder transformer workloads. The results also depend on GPU selection for pairing, where introducing PID modules in high-end HGX-H100 servers incurs 5.4--5.9$\times$ higher total carbon compared to A100 and H100 servers, due to their larger idle and embodied carbon. Introducing PID modules in higher-end GPU servers, compared to the A100-only baseline, increases (decreases) the total carbon-delay product (CDP) for encoder workloads (decoder workloads).

title: Stop Paying by the Letter: Accelerating Full-Chip RTL Simulation with Host-Side Tokenized Logging
summary:
Firmware diagnostic logging (printf) is an essential debug instrument in full-chip SoC design verification, yet it imposes a heavy tax on cycle-accurate RTL simulation: formatting a 30-character, 1-argument message on a simulated CPU and serializing it through an MMIO aperture costs 3.04 to 15.23 $μ$s per call (15.27 $μ$s unweighted / 15.08 $μ$s print-weighted critical-path mean on Suite A). Unlike embedded tokenizers that target flash footprint and wire bytes with offline decoding, RTL simulation is governed by a two-regime cost function---cross-fabric SoC paths are dominated by MMIO bus stalls (84.7% of call latency) whereas local subsystem paths are dominated by on-core vsprintf formatting (61.7%)---and requires live, zero-simulation-time string reconstruction to drive UVM scoreboards.
  We present a host-side in-simulation tokenized logging architecture for heterogeneous multi-core SoCs that eliminates both bottlenecks with zero firmware call-site edits. Using link-time ELF format-string virtual addresses as tokens over a fixed 32-bit word-aligned slot protocol across Arm, RISC-V, and DSP cores, on-core logging collapses to a single-pass specifier scan and $(1+S)$ MMIO word writes. This removes all on-core radix conversion ($C_{\mathrm{fmt}} \to 0$), 85.0%--94.5% of deployed bus transactions, 84.6%--93.3% of MMIO bus-stall cycles, and 63.5%--90.9% of total on-core logging cycles ($2.74\times$--$11.03\times$), while a SystemVerilog monitor reconstructs bit-exact strings in zero simulated cycles ($Δt_{\mathrm{sim}} = 0$). Across 858 matched full-chip test pairs (1,716 paired runs across 1,972 runs), we achieve 100% output parity with zero simulator memory overhead, saving 1,314.85 CPU hours (-26.18%) per regression pass, cutting median test CPU time by 41.51% (Suite A) and 21.33% (Suite B), and shrinking traces by 42.84% and waveforms by 28.82%.

title: M3D-FLOW: A Monolithic 3-D-Stackable Processing-Near-DRAM Architecture for Generative Normalizing Flow Applications
comment: 13 pages, 12 figures. Presented in CASES 2026 as a part of ESWEEK 2026. Accepted for publication in IEEE TCAD
summary: Normalizing Flows (NFs) have shown strong results in generative modeling, recently reaching state-of-the-art image generation performance. However, their repetitive, sequential operations limit the computational and memory efficiency achievable with GPUs and TPUs. We propose M3D-FLOW, a novel monolithic 3D-stackable (M3D) DRAM-based processing-near-memory (PNM) architecture that eliminates memory bottlenecks using a Cu-Cu hybrid-bonded logic die integrated with an M3D DRAM die. The M3D DRAM provides dense bank integration and a tiered organization with variable access latencies that M3D-FLOW exploits for the efficient processing of different NF workloads. To maximize compute density while minimizing area, energy, and thermal overhead, M3D-FLOW employs hybrid binary--stochastic floating-point multipliers, performing mantissa multiplication in the stochastic domain and exponent operations in the binary domain. A pipelined execution strategy maps sequential NF stages across dynamically partitioned PE groups, and together with the stochastic hardware, enables M3D-FLOW to achieve at least $6.6\times$ higher performance and $3\times$ better energy efficiency than prior PNM accelerators, with only a 2.2% bits-per-dimension (BPD) increase over bfloat16 and 4.1% over FP32. An analysis of stochastic hardware variants further shows that shorter stochastic bitstreams reduce execution time by up to $3.3\times$ at the cost of higher approximation error, providing a concrete design guide for latency--accuracy trade-offs.

title: Green Light: Carbon-Aware Design of Photonic Transformer Accelerators at the Edge
summary: Migrating transformer inference to the edge requires sustainability considerations that encompass both operation and manufacturing, rather than operational energy alone. Silicon photonics enables high-bandwidth, low-energy matrix multiplication; however, existing microring-resonator-based Dot Product Unit (DPU) organizations have been tailored to convolutional computations and evaluated using analog signaling without accounting for embodied carbon footprints. We adapt three DPU organizations (AMW, MAW, and MWA) to transformer inference workloads and extend each organization to stochastic signaling, yielding six organizations in total. We then calculate their embodied and operational carbon per inference. Across five transformer models and four foundry grids, the photonic system achieves improvements of four, four, and six orders of magnitude in Energy-Delay, Carbon-Delay, and Carbon-Energy Product, respectively, relative to CPUs, while also being compared against H100 SXM5 GPU and TPU v5p baseline systems. Analog-to-stochastic conversion increases die area by 4.3-4.6x and embodied carbon by 4.4-4.8x, while reducing operational energy by approximately 91% and causing embodied carbon to equal or exceed operational carbon per inference. Importantly, the DPU organization and signaling scheme, rather than the foundry grid, are the key determinants of carbon impact. Consequently, the fastest organization (MWA) is not necessarily the most carbon-efficient, whereas MAW-Stochastic offers a favorable balance between sustainability and performance.

title: Interflow: Breaking the Offline-Online Barrier for Private AI at the Edge
summary: Privacy-preserving machine learning (PPML) offers a promising path toward bringing powerful AI services to the edge without exposing sensitive user data. However, its practical deployment remains constrained by the high communication, computation, and data-movement costs of secure multi-party computation (MPC), particularly during nonlinear inference. Existing MPC systems typically decouple input-independent correlated randomness generation from online execution, creating substantial memory pressure to buffer single-use cryptographic data. Moreover, limited storage can force a stop-and-refill execution pattern that repeatedly stalls the pipeline to replenish these buffers, bringing randomness generation back onto the critical path. We propose Interflow, an algorithm-hardware co-design that rethinks this separation by batch-wise processing and pipelining correlated-randomness generation with online execution: while the current batch consumes pre-generated randomness to execute secure nonlinear operations, correlation generation proceeds concurrently for the next batch. By leveraging interleaved execution, efficient data movement, and hardware acceleration, the design transforms preprocessing from a serialized, storage-intensive offline phase into a continuously overlapped pipeline that generates correlated randomness closer to the point of consumption, reducing memory footprint and data movement overhead. Implemented on the Zynq UltraScale+ ZCU102, Interflow improves nonlinear evaluation throughput by up to 1.55x for CNN operators and 1.48x for transformer operators. It achieves up to 1.26x speedup for ResNet-50 and up to 1.21x speedup for BERT-base, and reduces memory footprint by up to 37%, compared with baseline frameworks.

title: ZKPU: Zero-Knowledge Processing Unit for Heterogeneous Workloads
summary:
Zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs) have become a fundamental building block for privacy-preserving computation, blockchain systems, and verifiable machine learning. Modern ZKP protocols span two distinct families: curve-based protocols, which rely on large finite-field arithmetic, and hash-based protocols, which operate over native 64-bit fields. Existing hardware accelerators are specialized for one protocol family because they are built on operand-scanning Montgomery multiplication, resulting in fixed-width datapaths, poor utilization across heterogeneous operand widths, and limited scalability.
  This paper presents \emph{ZKPU}, a Zero-Knowledge Processing Unit for heterogeneous ZKP workloads. ZKPU introduces a new compute paradigm by co-designing finely integrated product scanning (FIPS) Montgomery multiplication with a reconfigurable Twin Systolic Fabric (TSF), enabling modular multiplication at arbitrary widths in 64-bit increments. Combined with a fine-grained Deque buffer, on-chip twiddle-factor generator, and memory-efficient MSM preprocessing strategy, ZKPU provides a unified architecture for both curve-based and hash-based protocols. Evaluation using Groth16 and Plonky2 shows that ZKPU achieves up to $144\times$ speedup for NTT, $13.6\times$ for MSM, and approximately $7.2\times$ end-to-end application speedup over state-of-the-art accelerators, while being the first architecture to efficiently support both protocol families on a single reconfigurable hardware platform.

title: DiffRMST: A GPU-Accelerated Fully Differentiable Rectilinear Minimum Spanning Tree Wirelength Model for Global Placement
summary: Analytical global placement requires a differentiable wirelength objective that accurately reflects routed interconnect cost. The widely used half-perimeter wirelength (HPWL) is efficient but overlooks the internal topology of multi-pin nets. The rectilinear Steiner minimum tree (RSMT) provides higher fidelity, but its underlying decision problem is NP-complete, and its discrete construction precludes direct use in gradient-based optimization. The rectilinear minimum spanning tree (RMST) offers a polynomial-time alternative, but remains nondifferentiable because of minimization over discrete spanning trees. To address these limitations, we present DiffRMST, a fully differentiable RMST wirelength model for analytical global placement. DiffRMST combines spatial smoothing with a log-sum-exp relaxation to define a continuous distribution over spanning trees. Based on the Kirchhoff matrix-tree theorem, the partition function and edge marginals can be computed without explicit tree enumeration, enabling a closed-form topology-aware gradient for placement optimization. For efficient integration into analytical placement, we further develop a fused forward-backward operator with parallel CPU and GPU implementations. On the ISPD2019 benchmark suite, our method reduces RMST, RSMT, and routed wirelength by an average of 5.0%, 3.2%, and 3.5%, respectively, compared with the weighted-average baseline, while maintaining acceptable runtime. Furthermore, the GPU implementation achieves an average $14.7\times$ speedup in global placement over its eight-thread CPU counterpart.

title: RPolyPlan: A Unified Global Floorplanning and Legalization Framework for Rectilinear Soft Modules
summary: Floorplanning with rectilinear soft modules improves area utilization and wirelength by allowing modules to adapt to rectilinear polygon (RPoly) shapes. Existing methods typically construct rectilinear polygons through incremental refinement after obtaining a rectangular global solution, which confines polygon exploration to the neighborhood induced by the initial floorplan. This paper presents RPolyPlan, a unified framework for outline-free and fixed-outline floorplanning that directly incorporates continuously deformable rectilinear polygons into global floorplanning. To enable direct polygon optimization, we introduce a structured continuous representation and a differentiable polygon shaping model that dynamically optimizes rectilinear module shapes based on overlaps, making continuous shape optimization feasible for gradient-based global floorplanning. An augmented Lagrangian formulation robustly handles the coupled inequality constraints, provides theoretical convergence guarantees, and reduces dependence on manual penalty-parameter tuning. During legalization, minimum-cost flow and rectangular decomposition determine the target areas of subrectangles, and horizontal and vertical constraint graphs encode their geometric relations. The resulting convex legalization formulation satisfies the area, shape, separation, connectivity, and outline constraints while minimizing either the chip area or the displacement from the global floorplanning solution. Experiments on the GSRC, MCNC, and ICCAD 2023 contest benchmarks demonstrate that RPolyPlan reduces HPWL over the evaluated state-of-the-art methods by 7% and 6% in fixed-outline and outline-free experiments, respectively.
